chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father and Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Ibn Abi Umayr and Safwan ibn Yahya, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
I asked him about a person in ihram who looked at his wife and emitted pre-seminal fluid (madh) or seminal fluid (mani) while he was in ihram. He said: 'There is no penalty upon him.'

This is if his looking was without lust, because whenever he looked at her with lust and emitted fluid, the penalty of the blood of a camel (dam jazoor) is upon him. That which indicates this is what Mism'ab Abu Sayyar narrated from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) in the narration which we narrate later, if God wills.

The Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) said: And likewise, if he carried her and from him occurred what we mentioned, there is no penalty upon him, unless he presses her to himself with lust and emits seminal fluid, in which case the penalty of the blood of a sheep (dam shah) becomes obligatory upon him.

key_terms.دَمُ جَزُورٍ: The blood of a camel (a specific sacrificial penalty)
key_terms.دَمُ شَاةٍ: The blood of a sheep (a specific sacrificial penalty)
key_terms.مُحْرِمٌ: A person in the state of ihram (ritual consecration) for Hajj or Umrah

ai.seo_question: What is the penalty for a pilgrim in ihram who looks at his wife with lust?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the distinction between mere visual contact and lustful intent (*shahwah*) in determining the *kaffarah* (expiation) for a pilgrim in *ihram*. It establishes that unintentional emission incurs no penalty, while lustful gazing triggers the heavier penalty of a camel's blood, whereas physical embrace with lust results in the lighter penalty of a sheep's blood, reflecting the gradation of fault in Shia jurisprudence.
